lesson.title: Counting Without Double Counting: The Addition Rule
lesson.summary: The general addition rule, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) minus P(A and B), fixes the double counting that happens when two overlapping events are added together directly.
lesson.body:
The addition rule in its full generality answers the question, what is the probability that A or B happens, for any two events, whether or not they are disjoint. The rule states P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) minus P(A and B). When A and B happen to be disjoint, as in the previous chapter, P(A and B) equals zero, and the formula collapses back down to the simple version already covered, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). The general version is not a different rule so much as the same idea with a correction term added back in for the case the earlier chapter deliberately avoided: events that do overlap.

That correction term exists to fix a specific counting error. If A and B share some outcomes, adding P(A) and P(B) directly counts every outcome that belongs to both events twice, once as part of A and once as part of B, when it should only be counted once toward the probability of A or B happening. Subtracting P(A and B) removes exactly one of those two duplicate counts, leaving each outcome in the combined event counted precisely once, no matter whether it belongs to A alone, B alone, or both.

A picture helps make this concrete even without drawing one. Imagine two overlapping circles inside a rectangle representing the full sample space, one circle for A and one for B, with a lens shaped region in the middle where they overlap. The total shaded area covered by at least one circle is not the sum of the two circle areas, since that sum counts the lens shaped overlap twice, once from each circle. The correct shaded area is the sum of the two circle areas minus the overlap counted once too many, which is exactly what the addition rule formula computes in numbers rather than area.

Consider drawing one card from a standard 52 card deck and let A be the event the card is a heart and B be the event the card is a face card, meaning a jack, queen, or king of any suit. These events are not disjoint, since the jack, queen, and king of hearts belong to both groups. There are 13 hearts, so P(A) = 13/52. There are 12 face cards total across all four suits, so P(B) = 12/52. The overlap, hearts that are also face cards, consists of exactly three cards, the jack, queen, and king of hearts, so P(A and B) = 3/52. The general addition rule gives P(A or B) = 13/52 + 12/52 minus 3/52, which equals 22/52, or 11/26. This can be checked by direct counting: 13 hearts plus the 9 face cards that are not hearts, since 3 of the 12 face cards were already counted as hearts, gives 13 + 9 = 22 cards satisfying A or B, confirming the formula's answer.

The addition rule handles the or question completely, but it depends on already knowing P(A and B), the probability of both events happening together, which so far has only been computed by direct counting from a table or a listed sample space. The next two chapters build a real tool for finding P(A and B) directly from P(A) and P(B) alone, starting with the clean case where the two events do not affect each other at all.
